Most authors agree that the Bankart lesion is the most commonly observed pathological lesion in recurrent subluxation or dislocation of the shoulder.
Bankarts lesion involves the—of the glenoid labrum: Anterior lip.

Reference: Page 56, Section: Lesions Anoctated with Recurrent Dislocation & Page 69, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Dynamic stabilisers of shoulder joint? (AIMS Nov 2013)
questions.explanation:
Four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis and teres minor.
They are dynamic stabilisers of shoulder.
Their impingement causes painful arc syndrome.

Reference: Page 55, Section: SHOULDER ANATOMY & Page 69, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: For long the muscle was not given its due importance and was called Forgotten muscle of rotator cuff which one is it? (AIMS May 2013)
questions.explanation:
Subscapularis (Forgotten tendon).

Reference: Page 55, Section: SHOULDER ANATOMY

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Most common muscle damaged in rotator cuff: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Supraspinatus (Most commonly damaged).

Reference: Page 55, Section: SHOULDER ANATOMY

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Painful arc syndrome is caused by impingement of: (NEET Pattern 2013) (AIMS May 2013)
questions.explanation:
Their impingement causes painful arc syndrome.
Painful arc syndrome is seen in all except: Complete tear of supraspinatus.
It is anterior shoulder pain in 60-120° of glenohumeral abduction. It can be cause by: Chronic supraspinatus tendinitis (most common), Calcification of supraspinatus tendon, Partial (not complete) tears of supraspinatus tendon, Fracture of greater tuberosity, Subacromial bursitis.

Reference: Page 55, Section: SHOULDER ANATOMY & Page 146, Section: PAINFULARC SYNDROME

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Rotator cuff muscle all are true except:
questions.explanation:
Four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis and teres minor.

Reference: Page 55, Section: SHOULDER ANATOMY

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Lift off test is done for: (AIMS May 2012, AIPC 2010)
questions.explanation:
Lift Off Test (Gerber's test): Lift off test is done to assess the strength of subscapularis muscle and detect a rupture of the subscapularis tendon.

Reference: Page 55, Section: Lift Off Test (Gerber's test) & Page 69, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Rotator interval is between: (MAHE 2005, AIMS 06, JIPMER 02)
questions.explanation:
Rotator interval is interval between leading edge of supraspinatus and superior edge of subscapularis. Coracohumeral ligament passes with in rotator interval.

Reference: Page 55, Section: SHOULDER ANATOMY & Page 69, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Muscle crossing through the shoulder joint is: (NIMHANS 98, PGI 95)
questions.explanation:
The tendon of the long head of biceps brachii muscle passes superiorly through the joint and restricts upward movement of humeral head on glenoid cavity.

Reference: Page 55, Section: SHOULDER ANATOMY & Page 69, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Weakest portion of shoulder joint capsule is: (PGI 93, AI 92, AIMS 90)
questions.explanation:
The inferior part of shoulder joint capsule is the weakest area.
Shoulder is weakest inferiorly but dislocates anteriorly because it is the direction of force that decides the dislocation but never the anatomical weakness for a particular joint.

Reference: Page 55, Section: SHOULDER ANATOMY & Page 70, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Hill-Sachs lesion in recurrent shoulder dislocation is: (AIMS 1992) (JIPMER 1992)

options.text: Rupture of tendon of supraspinatus muscle

questions.explanation:
A humeral head impaction fracture can be produced as the shoulder is dislocated anteriorly, and the humeral head is impacted against the rim of the glenoid at the time of dislocation. This Hill-Sachs lesion is a defect in the posterolateral aspect of the humeral head.

Reference: Page 57, Section: Lesions Anoctated with Recurrent Dislocation & Page 70, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Commonest type of shoulder dislocation: (NEET Pattern 2013 PCI 87)
questions.explanation:
Anterior Dislocation of Shoulder-Most Common Type of Shoulder Dislocation.
Types: Subcoracoid > Preglenoid > Sublacicular.

Reference: Page 58, Section: Anterior Dislocation of Shoulder & Page 71, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Uncomplicated shoulder dislocation most commonly occurs in the following direction: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Anterior Dislocation of Shoulder-Most Common Type of Shoulder Dislocation.

Reference: Page 58, Section: Anterior Dislocation of Shoulder

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Nerve injured in anterior dislocation of shoulder: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Most commonly injured nerve in anterior dislocation of shoulder is circumflex branch of axillary nerve. The injury to nerve is usually neuropraxia.

Reference: Page 58, Section: Anterior Dislocation of Shoulder

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Neglected shoulder dislocation in a young labourer is: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Neglected shoulder dislocation—surgically managed.

Reference: Page 59, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: In Recurrent Anterior dislocation of shoulder, the movements that causes dislocation is: (AIIMS Nov 2011, Andhra 99,94, KA 97, AI 1989)
questions.explanation:
Anterior dislocation: Abduction and External rotation force.
Recurrent Anterior Dislocation - Abduction and External rotation force.

Reference: Page 58, Section: MODE OF INJURY CAUSING SHOULDER DISLOCATION & Page 247, Section: 7. UPPER LIMB TRAUMATOLOGY

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Recurrent dislocations are least commonly seen in: (AI 2009, Delhi 94)
questions.explanation:
Recurrent dislocation is most common in shoulder joint, accounting for nearly 50% of all dislocations. Second common joint for recurrent dislocation is patella and rarest joint to dislocate is ankle.

Reference: Page 58, Section: MODE OF INJURY CAUSING SHOULDER DISLOCATION & Page 71, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: All are related to recurrent shoulder dislocation except: (AIIMS May 2006, TN 2000, KA 98, UP 02, Karnataka 89)
questions.explanation:
Differences between recurrent and non- recurrent anterior dislocation:
Bankarts lesion: Recurrent - Common; Non-recurrent - Uncommon.
Hill-Sachs lesion: Recurrent - Common; Non-recurrent - Uncommon.
Lax capsule: Recurrent - Common; Non-recurrent - Uncommon.
Associated Injuries (Nerve injury Rotator cuff injury/Fractures): Recurrent - Rare; Non-recurrent - Common.

Reference: Page 58, Section: Differences between recurrent and non- recurrent anterior dislocation

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Traumatic glenohumeral instability in one direction with Bankarts lesion are treated by: (NIMHANS 2003)
questions.explanation:
Treatment of traumatic unidirectional instability Surgery.
Treatment of non-traumatic multidirectional instability Rehabilitation.

Reference: Page 71, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Following anterior dislocation of the shoulder, a patient develops weakness of flexion at elbow and lack of sensation over the lateral aspect forearm; nerve injured is: (AI 2001)
questions.explanation:
The most common complication of anterior dislocation of shoulder is axillary (circumflex) nerve injury. There is consequent paralysis of the deltoid muscle, with a small area of anaesthesia at the lateral aspect of the upper arm.
However, in this question the sensation are lost on lateral aspect of forearm (not arm). Lateral side of forearm has sensory supply from lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm, a branch of musculocutaneous nerve. Musculocutaneous nerve also suplies the biceps brachii (a flexor of elbow joint).
Therefore, musculocutaneous nerve injury will cause sensory loss over lateral aspect of the forearm with weakness of flexion at elbow.

Reference: Page 71, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Nerve injured inferior dislocation of shoulder: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Inferior dislocation also axillary nerve involvement is commonest.
Potentially serious consequences, e.g. neurovascular damage is quite common. (Axillary nerve injured).

Reference: Page 58, Section: MODE OF INJURY CAUSING SHOULDER DISLOCATION & Page 71, Section: INFERIOR DISLOCATION OF SHOULDER

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Luxatio erecta: (TN 98)
questions.explanation:
Inferior (Downward/subglenoid) dislocation of shoulder is known as luxatio erecta.
It is caused by severe hyper abduction force.

Reference: Page 59, Section: INFERIOR DISLOCATION OF SHOULDER & Page 71, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: 40-year-old male who was unconscious and presented with Bilateral Addiction and internal rotation of shoulder: (AllMS Nov 2012)
questions.explanation:
Mechanism of Injury Indirect force producing marked internal rotation and adduction, most commonly during a fit, convulsion or an electric shock.
The classical clinical feature is arm is held in medial rotation and is locked in that position, and an examiner can not externally rotate it.

Reference: Page 59, Section: POSTERIOR DISLOCATION OF SHOULDER-OFTEN MISSED CLINICALLY & Page 72, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: In posterior dislocation of shoulder hill sash lesion is seen in: (Al 2012)
questions.explanation:
Reverse Hill Sach's Lesion may be seen.
(RAMP)—Reverse Hill Sachs—Anteromedial humeral head-posterior dislocation of shoulder.

Reference: Page 59, Section: POSTERIOR DISLOCATION OF SHOULDER & Page 247, Section: 7. UPPER LIMB TRAUMATOLOGY

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Which is true about shoulder dislocation? (MAHE 2003, TN 98)

options.text: Anterior dislocation is common than posterior
Fixed medial rotation in posterior dislocation
Kocher's manoeuvre is effective in anterior dislocation

questions.explanation:
Anterior Dislocation of Shoulder-Most Common Type of Shoulder Dislocation.
Posterior dislocation: The classical clinical feature is arm is held in medial rotation and is locked in that position.
Commonly used reduction techniques are Stimson's gravity method, Hippocratic method and Kocher's method.

Reference: Page 58, Section: Anterior Dislocation of Shoulder & Page 59, Section: POSTERIOR DISLOCATION OF SHOULDER

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Which is true regarding shoulder dislocation? (SCPGI 2002, NIMHANS 99)

options.text: Pain is severe in anterior dislocation
Radiography may be misleading in posterior dislocation

questions.explanation:
POSTERIOR DISLOCATION OF SHOULDER- OFTEN MISSED CLINICALLY.
Clinical Presentation often missed clinically.
Investigation Reliance is placed on a single A-P X-ray which may look almost normal.

Reference: Page 59, Section: POSTERIOR DISLOCATION OF SHOULDER & Page 72, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Which of the following is test of posterior glenohumeral instability: (AllMS May 10, 09)
questions.explanation:
Posterior Instability (Adduction and internal rotation force): Jerk (provocative) test, Posterior apprehension test, Posterior clunk test, Push-Pull test.

Reference: Page 60, Section: TEST FOR EVALUATION OF GLENOHUMERAL JOINT INSTABILITY & Page 72, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has a history of recurrent dislocation of the right shoulder. On examination, the orthopedician puts the patient in the supine position and abducts his arm to 90° with the bed as the fulcrum and then externally rotates it but the boy does not allow the test to be performed. The test done by the orthopedician is: (AIIMS May 2001)
questions.explanation:
Anterior Instability: Anterior Apprehension Tests.
In general these maneuver mimics the positioning of subluxation or dislocation, application of anterior directed force to the humeral head from the back or abduction and external rotation of arm results in patients apprehension that the joint will dislocate. And the patient does not allow the test to be performed.

Reference: Page 60, Section: TEST FOR EVALUATION OF GLENOHUMERAL JOINT INSTABILITY & Page 73, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Most common bone to fracture in body: (Neet Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Clavicle is the most common fractured bone (over all) in adults and during birth.

Reference: Page 60, Section: Clavicle Fracture & Page 73, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Shoulder X-ray highest bony landmark is: (Neet Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
X-ray shoulder highest bony landmark is acromion.

Reference: Page 73, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: The most common bone fractured during birth: (CMC2002,MP1998)
questions.explanation:
Clavicle is the most common fractured bone (over all) in adults and during birth.

Reference: Page 60, Section: Clavicle Fracture & Page 73, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Clavicular fracture is usually treated by: (UP 2001, Tamil Nadu 1999, Andhra 99, JIPMER 87)
questions.explanation:
Sling immobilization/Figure of eight bandage is adequate nonoperative treatment for most isolated clavicle fractures.

Reference: Page 60, Section: Clavicle Fracture & Page 73, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Velpeau bandage and Sling and Swathe splint are used in? (AIIMS Nov 08)
questions.explanation:
Valpeau bandage (dressing) is used in acromioclavicular dislocation, fracture clavicle and shoulder dislocation but it is most effective in acromioclavicular dislocation as it pushes lateral end of shoulder down wards and arm upwards, and thus helps maintaining reduction.

Reference: Page 60, Section: ACROMIOCLAVICULAR DISLOCATION & Page 73, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Which of the following is least likely associated with vascular injury? (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
Fracture supracondylar humerus is: Most common fracture associated with vascular injury. Most common fracture to involve brachial artery. (10% cases).

Reference: Page 64, Section: Complications of Fracture Supracondylar Humerus

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Nerve injured in fracture of medial epicondyle of humerus: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
Injury to ulnar nerve: Fracture medial epicondyle humerus.
The ulnar nerve passes just behind the medical epicondyle. So, the fracture would lead to injury of ulnar nerve.

Reference: Page 61, Section: Injury & Page 159, Section: ULNAR NERVE INJURY

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Proximal humerus fracture which has maximum chances of avascular necrosis: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Four-part fractures are at very high risk for development of complete osteonecrosis of the humeral head, resulting in functional limitation.

Reference: Page 61, Section: FRACTURES OF SURGICAL NECK Humerus & Page 74, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Trauma to neck of humerus, nerve damaged: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Fracture surgical neck humerus: Axillary nerve.

Reference: Page 61, Section: Injury

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Posterior Elbow dislocation most common nerve involved is: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Associated soft tissue injuries may involve the brachial artery, ulnar nerve (most commonly), median and radial nerve.

Reference: Page 64, Section: Elbow Dislocation & Page 74, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Treatment of choice for fracture neck of humerus in a 70-year-old male: (PGI 2000, UP 2K, AIIMS June 1999, PGI 94, MAHE 96)
questions.explanation:
Most nondisplaced fractures can be treated with a short period of sling immobilization. Early range of motion has been shown to improve functional outcomes. (This is the case with elderly patients with impacted fractures).
Elderly osteoporotic females are usually involved. In such cases it is usually impacted.

Reference: Page 61, Section: FRACTURES OF SURGICAL NECK Humerus & Page 74, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Which of the following movements will be affected if the greater tubercle of the humerus is lost: (AIIMS Nov 2000)
questions.explanation:
Two-part fractures of the greater tuberosity are best treated with open reduction and internal fixation if displaced more than 3-5mm because there is increased risk of disability in patients who require overhead function especially abduction and external rotation. (Supraspinatus Assists deltoid in abduction and Infraspinatus/Teres minor - Laterally (externally) rotates arm and all these are attached on greater tuberosity).

Reference: Page 61, Section: FRACTURES OF SURGICAL NECK Humerus & Page 74, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Fracture neck humerus is common in: (TN 97)
questions.explanation:
The incidence increases with age and in the elderly the cause is typically a low-energy injury. Elderly osteoporotic females are usually involved.

Reference: Page 61, Section: FRACTURES OF SURGICAL NECK Humerus & Page 74, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Hanging cast is used in: (NEET Pattern 2012 AIMS Dec 1995)
questions.explanation:
Humerus shaft fracture: Coaptation splint/Hanging cast is used for non-operative management.

Reference: Page 62, Section: HUMERAL SHAFT FRACTURE & Page 75, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: The most important cause of non-union of fracture of humeral shaft is: (Orissa 1990)
questions.explanation:
Humerus shaft fracture; The most common cause of delayed union or non- union is distraction at fracture site due to gravity and weight of plaster.

Reference: Page 62, Section: HUMERAL SHAFT FRACTURE & Page 75, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: First to appear amongst the ossification centres about the elbow is: (UP 2003, PGI 96, Assam 99)
questions.explanation:
Capillulum is the first ossification centre about the elbow to appear. It appears around 2 years of age.
The mnemonic "CRITOE" is helpful in remembering the progression of the radiographic appearance of ossification centre about the elbow in children: C: Capitellum - 2 years.

Reference: Page 62, Section: Elbow Anatomy & Page 76, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Three bony point relationship is maintained in: (AllMS June 2000, Dec 1995, Nov 93, May 93, 91)
questions.explanation:
Three point bony relationship is not disturbed in fracture supracondylar humerus as the fracture occurs above the level of these bony landmarks.
With disturbed (increased) intercondylar distance: 1. Fracture lateral epicondyle and condyle, 2. Fracture medial epicondyle and condyle, 3. Fracture intercondylar humerus.
With maintained intercondylar distance: 1. Fracture olecranon (i.e. upper end ulna), 2. Elbow dislocation (classical example).

Reference: Page 62, Section: Three Point Bony Landmarks In Elbow & Page 76, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Postero lateral anconeus triangle is formed by: (Jipmer 2000, KA 2001)

options.text: Head of radius, lateral epicondyle, medial epicondyle
Head of radius, lateral epicondyle, olecranon
Olecranon, medial epicondyle, neck of radius
Neck of radius, head of radius, lateral epicondyle

questions.answerText: Head of radius, lateral epicondyle, olecranon
questions.explanation:
Radial head, lateral epicondyle and tip of olecranon form a triangle over the posterolateral aspect of elbow joint. This space is occupied by anconeus muscle and so known as anconeus triangle.

Reference: Page 62, Section: Three Point Bony Landmarks In Elbow & Page 76, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: All of the following are complications of supra-condylar fracture of humerus in children, except: (AIIMS May 2014)
questions.explanation:
Complications of Fracture Supracondylar Humerus: 1. Malunion (Most Common Complication), 2. Vascular (brachial artery) injury, 3. Nerve injury, 4. Volkman's ischemia and compartment syndrome, 5. Elbow stiffness, 6. Myositis ossificans, 7. Avascular necrosis of trochlea. (rare), 8. Trayd ulnar nerve palsy.
Fracture supracondylar humerus is: Non-union is unknown.

Reference: Page 64, Section: Complications of Fracture Supracondylar Humerus & Page 65, Section: Fracture suprascapular humerus is

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Malunited Supracondylar fracture humerus causes: (NEET Pattern 2014, 2012)
questions.explanation:
Supracondylar fracture humerus - causes malunion hence cubitus varus and this fracture is above the growth plate hence static cubitus varus.

Reference: Page 62, Section: Three Point Bony Landmarks In Elbow & Page 77, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Supracondylar fracture true except: (AIIMS Nov, May 2013)

options.text: Distal segment displaced anterior is more common
Cubitus valgus malunion more common than varus

questions.explanation:
Most common type of supracondylar fracture - Extension type (~98% of all supracondylar fracture).
Most common type of distal fragment displacement in extension type fracture supracondylar humerus - "Posteromedial displacement with internal rotation".
Malunion Most Common Complication: Posteromedially displaced fracture tend to develop Cubitus varus (gun stock deformity).
Nerve injury (anterior interosseous n. > median n. > radial n > ulnar. n): These are usually neuropraxia, hence transient.

Reference: Page 63, Section: FRACTURE SUPRACONDYLAR HUMERUS & Page 64, Section: Complications of Fracture Supracondylar Humerus

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Late complication of elbow dislocation: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
Elbow dislocation: Myositis ossificans is late complication.

Reference: Page 64, Section: Elbow Dislocation & Page 77, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: True about supracondylar fracture of humerus:
questions.explanation:
Supracondylar humeral fractures in children are most common elbow injuries, especially in children aged 5-8 years. They account for 50-70% of all elbow fractures.
Most common type of supracondylar fracture - Extension type (~98% of all supracondylar fracture).

Reference: Page 63, Section: FRACTURE SUPRACONDYLAR HUMERUS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: In extension type of supracondylar fracture, the usual displacement is: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
Most common type of distal fragment displacement in extension type fracture supracondylar humerus - "Posteromedial displacement with internal rotation".

Reference: Page 63, Section: FRACTURE SUPRACONDYLAR HUMERUS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Deformity in posterior elbow dislocation: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
The most common dislocation is posterior or posterolateral and is usually the result of a fall with forearm supinated and the elbow either extended or partially flexed.
Clinical Feature: Elbow is held in Flexion.

Reference: Page 64, Section: Elbow Dislocation

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Commonest dislocation of elbow: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
The most common dislocation is posterior or posterolateral.

Reference: Page 64, Section: Elbow Dislocation & Page 77, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: What is seen on X-ray with posterior elbow dislocation: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Elbow dislocation: Coronoid process is posterior to humerus.

Reference: Page 64, Section: Elbow dislocation & Page 77, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: In posterior dislocation of elbow, most prominent part: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Most prominent part is olecranon in dislocated elbow.

Reference: Page 64, Section: Elbow dislocation & Page 77, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Early complication of elbow dislocation are all except: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Associated soft tissue injuries may involve the brachial artery, ulnar nerve (most commonly), median and radial nerve.
Myositis ossificans is late complication.

Reference: Page 64, Section: Elbow Dislocation

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Supracondylar fracture humerus treatment is: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Treatment is closed reduction and cast if it fails or if fracture is displaced than closed reduction and K- wire fixation.

Reference: Page 63, Section: Gartland Classification is used for Supracondylar Fractures & Page 78, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Elbow dislocation going into most commonly: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
The most common dislocation is posterior or posterolateral.

Reference: Page 64, Section: Elbow Dislocation

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Micro circulation blockade is a feature of: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
In acute compartment syndromes increased pressure in a close fascial space causes loss of microcirculation.

questions.stem: Excision of head of radius in a child should not be done because: (IIPMER 2001)

options.text: It produces instability of elbow joint
It leads to secondary Osteo arthritis of elbow
It causes subluxation of inferior radio-ulnar joint

questions.answerText: It causes subluxation of inferior radio-ulnar joint
questions.explanation:
Classically the head of radius should not be excised in children because. It will interfere with the synchronous growth of radius and ulnar producing wrist and elbow deformity. It leads to proximal radial migration and subluxation of inferior radio ulnar joint. It causes weakness of extremity and discomfort in distal radio-ulnar joint with heavy activities. May produce cubitus valgus deformity and instability.

questions.stem: Fracture of proximal forearm cast position is: (NEET Pattern 2013)

A fracture of shaft of radius at the junction of upper and middle thirds proximal to pronator teres is therefore situated between two groups of muscles. The proximal fragment has only supinators inserted into it and the distal fragment has only pronators. Thus causing supination of proximal fragment and pronation of distal fragment. Fractures of upper third of radius, therefore, should usually be immobilized with the hand and forearm supinated.

questions.explanation:
Complications of Colle's Fracture: Joint Stiffness: Finger stiffness is most common complication. Wrist, elbow, and shoulder are other joints to become stiff. Malunion is the 2nd most common complication and it leads to dinner fork deformity. Sudeck's osteo dystrophy/Reflex sympathetic dystrophy. Colle's fracture is the commonest cause of sudeck's dystrophy in upper limb. Rupture of extensor pollicis longus tendon. Carpal tunnel syndrome causing median nerve compression. Carpal instability. questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: A lady with Colle's fracture. The fracture healed but after few days patient develops pain and swelling over wrist and forearm, red hot and shiny skin and on X-Ray-patchy osteopenia. Diagnosis is? (AIIMS May 2013)
questions.explanation:
Sudeck's osteoneuro dystrophy/reflex sympathetic dystrophy/causalgia/algodystrophy/complex regional pain syndrome.
The most characteristic symptom is pain out of proportion to the inciting event in both severity and duration. It is often burning in character. Hence the term 'Causalgia' which means burning pain.
Swelling is the most consistent physical finding. It often begins in area of injury and is soft initially as the process continues, oedema gradually becomes firm and involves much broader area.
Stiffness and discoloration of skin (red, blue and/or pallor) are other classic signs.
The most common radiographic finding is localized osteopenia-increased blood flow to the bone.

Reference: Page 74, Section: SUDSECK'S OSTEONEURO DYSTROPHY & Page 88, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 7: Upper Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Sudeck's dystrophy symptoms are all except: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
The most common radiographic finding is localized osteopenia- increased blood flow to the bone.
Pain is the primary clinical feature of CRPS.

questions.stem: Denis gave how many columns theory to define stability of spine: (AIMS Nov 2012)
questions.explanation:
Denis' Three-Column Theory: Proposed by Francis Denis, three-column concept divides a spinal segment into three parts: Anterior, middle, and posterior columns. The anterior column comprises the anterior longitudinal ligament and the anterior half of the vertebral body; the middle column comprises the posterior half of the vertebral body and the posterior longitudinal ligament; the posterior column comprises the pedicles, the facet joints and the supraspinous ligaments. Significance: If 2 out of 3 columns are involved it is labelled as unstable spinal injury.

Reference: Page 80, Section: Explanation & Page 81, Section: Denis' Three-Column Theory

questions.stem: Which is not a feature of cervical syringomyelia: (AllMS Nov 2012)
questions.explanation:
Syringomyelia is a generic term referring to a disorder in which a cyst or cavity forms within the spinal cord. This cyst, called a syrinx, can expand and elongate over time, destroying the spinal cord. Cervical Syringomyelia has variable clinical presentations which include asymmetric weakness and atrophy of hands, lower limb spasticity, areflexia of upper extremity, dissociated sensory loss in the neck and arms (classic cape like distribution) and increased tone and hyperreflexia of lower limb. Thus there is wasting of hand and not hypertrophy.
Diagnostic modality is MRI.
Treatment is surgical.

Reference: Page 81, Section: Explanation & MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 8: Spinal Injury
questions.stem: In spinal shock: (NIMHANS 99)

options.text: Knee jerk is the first reflex to return
High thoracic lesions are commonly associated with more severe neurological deficits
Failure of return of cord activity within 48 hours is a very poor prognostic sign

questions.explanation:
SPINAL SHOCK: Some times physical energy of the injury mechanism causes immediate depolarization of axonal membranes in the neural tissue. This results in functional neurological deficit that exceeds the actual tissue disruption. This condition is referred to as spinal shock. The presence of spinal shock causes the absence of all reflexes. And it typically lasts upto 24-48 hours after the injury. The bulbocavernosus reflex is the reflex that returns first, thus marking the end of spinal shock.

Reference: Page 79, Section: SPINAL SHOCK & Page 81, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.stem: Complete transaction of the spinal cord at the C7 level produces all of the following effects except: (A12002)

options.text: Anaesthesia below the level of the lesion
Areflexia below the level of the lesion

questions.answerText: Areflexia below the level of the lesion
questions.explanation:
The diaphragm is innervated by two phrenic nerves that originate as branches of the cervical plexus in neck. This motor nerve to diaphragm arise from the anterior rami of cervical nerves C3, C4, C5 with major contribution coming from C4. So transaction of spinal cord at C7 level is not going to stop respiration but due to involvement of thoracic intercostal muscles and abdominal muscles, there will be some weakness of respiratory effort (i.e. limited respiratory effort). Deep tendon reflexes above the level of complete spinal cord injury will be spared; at the level of injury will be absent and below the level of injury will be exaggerated.

options.text: Anterior segment is not visualized adequately
Sciatic nerve injury in 10 percent in the cases

questions.answerText: Sciatic nerve injury in 10 percent in the cases
questions.explanation:
Kocher-Langenbeck Approach: This is a posterior approach used for all posterior wall, posterior column, and posterior column plus posterior wall fractures of acetabulum. It allows complete exposure of (posterior) retroacetabular surface caudally (distally) as far as the ischeal tuberosity. The greater and lesser sciatic notches are visualized. But the anterior and superior exposure is limited. Incidence of sciatic nerve injury is 2-6% (older studies explain wider range).

Reference: Page 91, Section: Vascular sign of Narath & Page 92, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 9: Pelvis and Hip Injury
questions.stem: Commonset dislocation of the hip is: (TN 92, 89)
questions.explanation:
Posterior Dislocation and Fracture-Dislocation-Dashboard injury It is the Most common hip dislocation (90%).

Reference: Page 90, Section: Posterior Dislocation and Fracture-Dislocation & Page 92, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 9: Pelvis and Hip Injury
questions.stem: In anterior dislocation of hip, the posture of lower limb will be: (AIMS N 99, Orissa 88) (Orissa 1990)
questions.explanation:
Anterior dislocations occur with the hip externally rotated and abducted. The degree of flexion at the time of injury determines the eventual position of the femoral head.

Reference: Page 91, Section: ANTERIOR DISLOCATION OF THE HIP & Page 92, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 9: Pelvis and Hip Injury
questions.stem: In per rectal examination, femoral head is palpable in: (Andhra 1998)
questions.explanation:
In central fracture dislocation of hip, femoral head is forced medially through the floor of acetabulum and can be palpated on per rectal examination.

Reference: Page 91, Section: CENTRAL DISLOCATION & Page 93, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 9: Pelvis and Hip Injury
questions.stem: A 33/M has history of RTA, now complaints of pain left hip. On examination there is Flexion External Rotation of left lower limb. There is 7cm shortening of left lower limb, there is a gluteal mass felt which moves with the movement of femoral shaft, which of the following is the diagnosis: (AI 2012)
questions.explanation:
Anterior dislocation is ruled out because it will have Flexion Abduction External Rotation with lengthening and anterior femoral head (Mass that moves with femur shaft is femur head).
Central dislocation is ruledout because it will have shortening and femur head palpable on per rectal examination.
Posterior dislocation will have Flexion Adduction and internal rotation with shortening and gluteal femoral head.
Associated fracture with dislocations do not have the classical deformities.
Posterior dislocation with fracture of head of femur: Shortening, Classical deformities of posterior dislocation not present, Head posterior (Gluteal), Pipkins type IV: Shortening and gluteal mass with atypical features.

Reference: Page 93, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: True about proximal fragment in supratrochanteric fracture is: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
SUBTROCHANTERIC FEMORAL FRACTURES: Russell and Taylor classification. There is flexion, abduction and external rotation of proximal fragment.

Reference: Page 98, Section: SUBTROCHANTERIC FEMORAL FRACTURES & Page 98, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Subtrochanteric fractures of femur can be treated by all of the following methods except: (Al 2005)
questions.explanation:
Smith Paterson triangled nail was used for internal fixation of fracture neck femur (not subtrochanteric femur).
Treatment of choice is cephalomedullary nail.

Reference: Page 98, Section: SUBTROCHANTERIC FEMORAL FRACTURES & Page 98, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: True Supracondylar fracture of femur: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
True Supracondylar fracture of femur is Type A.
Type A - Supracondylar fracture
Type B - Intercondylar fracture
Type C - Comminuted intercondylar fracture

Reference: Page 99, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS & Page 256, Section: 10. LOWER LIMB TRAUMATOLOGY

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: A child was given gallows traction. What is the diagnosis? (AIIMS May 2013)
questions.explanation:
Gallow traction: < 2 years of age and traction weight < 2 kg of weight can be used.
Treatment of choice for fracture shaft femur < 5-year of age is spica and not gallows traction.

Reference: Page 99, Section: Management Plan & Page 99, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Exsanguinating blood loss in: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
1 unit tibia, 2 units femur, 4-8 units pelvis.

Reference: Page 99, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Gallows traction is most optimum for: (AIIMS Nov 2013; NEET Pattern 2013; 2012)

options.text: Fracture shaft femur > 2 years of age
Fracture shaft femur < 2 years of age

questions.answerText: Fracture shaft femur < 2 years of age
questions.explanation:
Gallow traction: < 2 years of age and traction weight < 2 kg of weight can be used.

Reference: Page 99, Section: Management Plan & Page 99, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Why fracture shaft femur is early stabilised: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
1 unit tibia, 2 units femur, 4-8 units pelvis.

Reference: Page 99, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology

questions.explanation:
1 unit tibia, 2 units femur, 4-8 units pelvis.

Reference: Page 99, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Thomas splint most troubling is: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Thomas splint most troubling is: Ring, because it impinges against proximal thigh.

Reference: Page 99, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: In upper one third femoral shaft fracture, the displacement of proximal segment is: (CSE 1999, Rohtak 97)
questions.explanation:
Proximal Third Fracture: Proximal fragment flexes, abducts and externally rotates because of gluteus medius and iliopsoas. Distal fragment is adducted (adductor longus, minimus, magnus and pectineus).

Reference: Page 98, Section: Displacements In Fracture Shaft femur & Page 99, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Maximum shortening of lower limb is seen in: (AIIMS Dec 1995)
questions.explanation:
Lower limb injuries associated with maximum shortening are posterior dislocation of hip > fracture shaft femur > Fracture subtrochanteric femur > Intertrochanteric fracture > Fracture Neck Femur.

Reference: Page 99, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: The femur is fractured at birth at: (Rajashan 93)
questions.explanation:
Most common location: Upper 1/3rd of femur.

Reference: Page 99, Section: FRACTURE SHAFT FEMUR IN CHILDREN & Page 99, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Fat Embolism most common fracture associated is: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Fat embolism is a common phenomenon it is more commonly seen in patients with multiple fractures and in fractures involving lower limbs especially femur.

Reference: Page 99, Section: FAT EMBOLISM SYNDROME & Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Fat embolism syndrome is characterized by all except: (PGI June 09, Dec 07, 04, Rohtak 98)
questions.explanation:
Gurd's Minor Criteria (8): Tachycardia, Fever, Anemia, Thrombocytopenia, Fat globules in sputum, Fat globules in urine (Gurd Test), Increasing ESR, Retinal emboli.
Thrombocytopenia Is Seen In Fat Embolism.

Reference: Page 99, Section: Gurd's Minor Criteria & Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: A person with multiple injuries develops fever restlessness, tachycardia, tachypnea and subconjunctival rash after 48 hours of injury. The likely diagnosis is: (AIIMS Nov 2008)
questions.explanation:
The classical triad of fat embolism syndrome is: 1. Respiratory symptoms: Dyspnea or tachypnea. 2. Neurological symptoms: Confusion or disorientation. 3. Petechial rash: In axilla, neck, periumbical area, conjunctiva of lower lid, front and beck of chest, shoulder.

Reference: Page 99, Section: Clinical Presentation & Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Insal-Salvati index is used for: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
Insal-Salvati index is used for: Patella. This index is ratio of patellar tendon length to the length of patella (n) is between 0.8 to 1.2. <0.8 - Patella baja (low lying patella). >1.2 - Patella alta (high lying patella).

Reference: Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Bulge sign in knee joint is seen after how much fluid accumulation: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
Knee Effusion is tested by Patella Tap, Bulge sign (10-15 ml fluid), Balloon sign, Ballotement of patella.

Reference: Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Tube (Cylinder) cast is applied for the fracture of: (All India 2007)
questions.explanation:
Cylinder cast in full extension is given for undisplaced patella fractures OR knee injuries.

Reference: Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Transverse fracture of the patella with separation of fragments is best treated by: (PGI Dec 2006, 92, AIIMS 87, Kerala 87)

options.text: Open reduction with screw fixation of the fragments
Blind fixation of the two fragments with Kirschner-wire
Open reduction with Kirschner-wire fixation of the fragment with tension band wiring

questions.answerText: Open reduction with Kirschner-wire fixation of the fragment with tension band wiring
questions.explanation:
Displaced Transverse Fracture: Tension Band wiring by K-wires and stainless steel (SS) wire.

Reference: Page 99, Section: FRACTURE PATELLA & Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: A comminuted fracture of the Patella should be treated by: (Bihar 1989)
questions.explanation:
Comminuted Fracture: At least proximal third of patella is intact - Partial Patellectomy. Severe Comminution - Total Patellectomy.

Reference: Page 99, Section: FRACTURE PATELLA & Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Mechanism of injury in lateral condylar fracture of proximal tibia: (NEET Pattern 2013)

options.text: Strain of valgus knee with axial loading

questions.answerText: Strain of valgus knee with axial loading
questions.explanation:
Mechanism of injury in lateral condylar fracture of proximal tibia: Strain of valgus knee with axial loading.

Reference: Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Patellar tendon bearing cast is indicated in the following fracture: (AI 02)
questions.explanation:
Sarmiento PTB (patellar tendon bearing) plaster, is a carefully moulded patellar bearing below knee plaster which is used in fractures of shaft of tibia in the later stages of conservative treatment when the fracture is more stable (and sticky) and requires the stimulus of direct weight bearing.

Reference: Page 100, Section: Management of Fracture Tibia & Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: A patient has 2 months POP cast for tibial fracture of left leg. Now he needs mobilisation with a single crutch. You will use this crutch on which side: (AIIMS Nov 2000)
questions.explanation:
Use of Single Crutch: In the opposite side for Fracture both bone leg and Hip Pathology.

Reference: Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: In posterior compartment syndrome which passive movement causes pain? (AIIMS Nov 08)
questions.explanation:
Deeper muscles are more commonly involved and they go distal, e.g. flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus their ischemia can be tested by toe dorsiflexion and will be more specific than foot dorsiflexion.

Reference: Page 100, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Pronation of foot the joints that become parallel are: (AIMS Nov 2014)
questions.explanation:
Pronation of foot the joints that become parallel are: Talonavicular and calcaneocuboid.

Reference: Page 101, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Pilon Fracture is: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
Tibial Pilon Fracture: The terms tibial plafond fracture, pilon fracture, and distal tibial explosion fracture all have been used to describe intraarticular fractures of the distal tibia.

Reference: Page 101, Section: Tibial Pilon Fracture & Page 101, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Which of the following is a syndesmosis? (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Inferior tibio fibular joint is a syndesmosis.

Reference: Page 101, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Ankle sprain ligament involved is: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Lateral Collateral Ligament: It is a weak ligament, involved in over 90% of ankle ligament injuries. It has three parts: 1. Anterior talofibular - Most commonly injured, 2. Middle calcaneo fibular - 2nd most common injured, 3. Posterior talofibular - Torn in most severe injuries.

Reference: Page 101, Section: Lateral Collateral Ligament & Page 101, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: March fracture involves: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
March fracture is a stress fatigue fracture of second metatarsal neck > 3rd metatarsal neck.
Most common site for march fracture is 2nd metatarsal followed by third metatarsal.

Reference: Page 51, Section: Sites of Stress Fractures & Page 101, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Runners fracture involves: (NEET Pattern 2012)
questions.explanation:
Rarely fibula lower end (runners fracture).

Reference: Page 51, Section: Sites of Stress Fractures & Page 101, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Fracture involving both the malleoli is: (NIIMS 1992 PGI 91)
questions.explanation:
Potts fracture is bimalleolar fracture and cottons fracture is trimalleolar fracture.

Reference: Page 102, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Fracture of talus without displacement in X-ray would lead to: (PGI June 02)

options.text: Avascular necrosis of body of talus
Avascular necrosis of neck of talus

questions.explanation:
The osseous vessels enter the talus through its neck and run postero-laterally to supply the body of talus. Therefore, In displaced fracture of talus neck, the blood supply of body is cut off which results in avascular necrosis of the body of the talus.
Secondary Osteoarthritis of Subtalar > ankle joint occurs some years after injury in over 50% range (47-97%) of patients.

Reference: Page 102, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS & Complications

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Avascular necrosis is a complication of: (AI 1999)

options.text: Fracture of medial condyle of femur

questions.explanation:
Avascular necrosis of body is a common complication. The incidence varies with the severity of displacement: in type 1 -15%, in type II -50%, in type III -100%, type IV -100% AVN.

Reference: Page 102, Section: Complications & Page 102, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: One of the following fracture requires plaster of paris cast with equines position: (PAL 96)
questions.explanation:
Treatment: Undisplaced - Cast in Equinus. Displaced: Reduction and fixation.

Reference: Page 102, Section: FRACTURE TALUS (NECK) & Page 102, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: MC comp.of fracture talus is: (AIIMS May 1995)
questions.explanation:
Secondary Osteoarthritis of Subtalar > ankle joint occurs some years after injury in over 50% range (47-97%) of patients. This is regarded as the most common complication of fracture talus.

Reference: Page 102, Section: Complications & Page 102, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Most commonly injured tarsal bone: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
Calcaneum is the most commonly fractured tarsal bone.

Reference: Page 102, Section: FRACURE CALCANEUM & Page 104, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Long compression is used for which fracture:
questions.explanation:
Long compression is used for Calcaneum fracture.

Reference: Page 104, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Bohlers angle is for:
questions.explanation:
Tuber angle of Bohler (Tuber-joint angle): It is formed between a line drawn from highest points of anterior process and highest point of posterior facet and a line drawn tangentially to the superior edge of the tuberosity. It is normally between 20-40 degrees. Flattening/Reduction/Reversal of this angle indicates Weight bearing posterior facet has collapsed (intra-articular fracture) or Degree of proximal displacement of the tuberosity (intra-articular and extra-articular fracture both).

Reference: Page 102, Section: Radiological Feature of Fracture Calcanem & Page 104, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Fracture of calcaneus management depending upon: (PGI June 08)
questions.explanation:
Management of Calcaneal Fractures:
Plain X-rays done for calcaneal fractures include lateral, oblique and axial views. Axial view of calcaneum is Harris view. Brodens view is also used. CT is the investigation of choice.
Treatment are: 1. Conservative treatment for non-displaced or minimally displaced fractures with early range of motion. 2. Open reduction and internal fixation for joint depression fractures.

Reference: Page 104, Section: Management of Calcaneal Fractures & MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Bohler's angle is decreased in fracture of: (All India 2007, AllMS May 07) (AllMS May 2007, AIPG 2007)
questions.explanation:
Bohler's Tuber Joint Angle and Crucial Angle of Gissane are measured for Intra-articular Fractures of Calcaneum.
Flattening/Reduction/Reversal of this angle indicates Weight bearing posterior facet has collapsed (intra-articular fracture) or Degree of proximal displacement of the tuberosity.

Reference: Page 102, Section: Radiological Feature of Fracture Calcanem & Page 104, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Gissane's angle in intra-articular fracture of calcaneum: (MAHE 04, AMU 2002)
questions.explanation:
Crucial Angle of Gissane: Formed by two cortical struts extending laterally, one along the lateral margin of posterior facet and other extending to the beak of the calcaneus. Normally it is an obtuse angle of 95-105 degree. It increases in intra-articular fractures.

Reference: Page 102, Section: Crucial Angle of Gissane & Page 104, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Neutral triangle is seen radiologically in: (NIMS 2003)
questions.explanation:
Neutral Triangle of Calcaneum: Within the trabeculae of calcaneus lies the neutral triangle, an area directly below the distal edge of posterior facet. Base of the triangle is the weakest, most vulnerable portion of the calcaneum. Axial impaction of the talus into the calcaneum results in a vertical fracture through the neutral triangle, and it represents the primary fracture line.

Reference: Page 104, Section: Neutral Triangle of Calcaneum & Page 104, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Calcaneum is associated most commonly with which: (AllMS Feb 1997, Delhi 1992)
questions.explanation:
Calcaneum is the most commonly fractured tarsal bone and in most cases the mode of injury is fall from height over 20% of these patients suffer associated injury of Dorsolumbar spine (most common), pelvis or hip, base of skull, tibia and talus.

Reference: Page 104, Section: FALL FROM HEIGHT & Page 104, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Least common complication of fall from height is: (AllMS Dec 1994)
questions.explanation:
Calcaneum is the most commonly fractured tarsal bone and in most cases the mode of injury is fall from height over 20% of these patients suffer associated injury of Dorsolumbar spine (most common), pelvis or hip, base of skull, tibia and talus.

Reference: Page 104, Section: FALL FROM HEIGHT & Page 104, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Watson Jones'approach is done for? (AIIMS Nov 2008)
questions.explanation:
Watson-Jones is also a lateral approach to the hip joint, which can be used for hip replacement (although rarely used as more commonly used approaches are Moore's posterior and Hardinge's antero-lateral approach).

Reference: Page 104, Section: CHRONIC ANKLE INSTABILITY & Page 105, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology
questions.stem: Watson Jones'procedure is done for: (AIIMS Nov 2008)
questions.explanation:
Chronic ankle instability can be satisfactorily treated by WatsonJones procedure. In which reconstruction of ankle ligaments is carried out, using peronei tendons.

Reference: Page 104, Section: CHRONIC ANKLE INSTABILITY & Page 105, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.explanation:
March fracture: Fatigue fracture of the neck of 2nd and 3rd metatarsal.

Reference: Page 105, Section: Eponym & Page 105, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

Boxer's fracture: A fracture through the neck of the 5th metacarpal.

questions.explanation:
Bennet's fracture dislocation: Partial fracture of 1st metacarpal base with trapezium-metacarpal joint dislocation.

Reference: Page 105, Section: Eponym & Page 105, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology

Barton's fracture: Fracture through the articular surface of distal radius with subluxation of wrist.

Reference: Page 105, Section: Eponym & Page 106, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology

Colles fracture: Distal metaphyseal fracture of radius with dorsal displacement and angulation.

questions.stem: Chauffer's Fracture: (NEET Pattern 2012)

Chauffre's fracture: An intra-articular oblique fracture of the styloid process of the radius.

Reference: Page 105, Section: Eponym & Page 106, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

Tillaux fracture: Lower tibial epiphysis injury (anterolateral part).

Aviator's fracture: Fracture of neck of the talus.

Reference: Page 105, Section: Eponym & Page 106, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology

Bumper fracture: Comminuted depressed fracture of the lateral tibial condyle.

options.text: Fracture distal fibula with posterior dislocation of proximal fragment
Fracture distal fibula with dislocation of distal fragment

BosWorth Fracture: Fracture distal fibula with posterior dislocation of proximal fragment.

Cotton's fracture: Trimalleolar ankle fracture (medial, lateral and posterior malleolar) fracture.

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 10: Lower Limb Traumatology

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 13: Sports Injury
questions.stem: Patient presents with knee Problem. He gives history of injury during playing hockey 3 months back. On testing knee was unstable anteriorly in extension but was stable in 90 degrees of flexion probably injury involves: (AIMs May 2013)
questions.explanation:
The ACL ligament is the primary restraint to anterior tibial displacement, accounting for approximately 85% of the resistance to the anterior drawer test when the knee is at 90° of flexion and neutral rotation. Selective sectioning of the ACL has shown that the anteromedial band is tight in flexion, providing the primary restraint, whereas the posterolateral bulky portion of this ligament is tight in extension. The posterolateral bundle provides the principal resistance for hyperextension. Thus complete tear will have instability in both flexion and extension. Thus anteromedial tear will have instability in flexion only and posterolateral tear will have instability only in extension.

Reference: Page 118, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 13: Sports Injury
questions.stem: Anterolateral arthroscopy of knee is for: (NEET Pattern 2013)

options.text: To see the posterior cruciate ligament
To see the anterior portion of lateral meniscus
To see the periphery of the posterior horn of medial meniscus

questions.explanation:
Standard portals in knee arthroscopy:
Anterolateral portal: Almost all the structures within the knee joint can be seen except the posterior cruciate ligament, the anterior portion of the lateral meniscus, and the periphery of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus in tight knees. Located 1 cm above the joint line, 1 cm lateral to the margin of the patellar tendon.
Anteromedial portal: Used for additional viewing of lateral compartment and insertion of probe for palpation of medial and lateral compartment structures. Placed 1 cm above the medial joint line, 1 cm inferior to the tip of patella, and 1 cm medial to the edge of the patella.
Posteromedial portal: Located on the soft triangular soft spot formed by the posteromedial edge of the femoral condyle and the posteromedial edge of tibia. Used for viewing the posteromedial structures and for repair or removal of the displaced posterior horn of meniscal tears and for posteromedial loose body removal.
Superolateral portal: Used for diagnostically viewing the dynamics of patella-femoral joint, excision of medial plicae. Located just lateral to the quadriceps tendon and about 2.5 cm superior to the superolateral corner of patella.

Reference: Page 118, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.stem: Lateral blow to knee with fracture in intercondylar area structured injured is: (AIIMS Nov 2012)
questions.explanation:
Mechanism of injury: 1. Valgus force - MCL, 2. Varus force - LCL, 3. Backward force - PCL, 4. Twisting injury (medial and lateral) - meniscus, 5. Anterior - ACL, 6. Combination of Valgus in Flexion with twist injuries the structure in following order: MCL than ACL, and last menisci.
Abduction or valgus force at flexed knee with rotational component is most common mechanism causing ligament injury at knee and if all forces are combined ACL is most commonly injured and if there is only rotational component than it causes menisci injury medial meniscus >lateral meniscus.
Thus rotation with valgus causes ACL injury.
In this question there is a point given-fracture at intercondylar which is the site of insertion of ACL. Hence ACL is the answer.

questions.stem: A patient met with Road Traffic Accident and developed knee pain. DIAL test was positive. Structure injured is: (AIIMS May 2012/Nov 2010)
questions.explanation:
Dial Test or Tibial External Rotation Test: This is the test for posterolateral instability. The tibia is externally rotated on femur first at 30° flexion and then at 90° flexion. Comparison is made with the normal side. An increase in external rotation of greater than 10° indicates pathology. Increase in external rotation at 30° of flexion but not at 90° indicates an isolated posterolateral corner injury and at both 30° and 90° of flexion indicates injury of both posterior cruciate ligament and posterolateral corner.

options.text: Varus/valgus stress test in full flexion

Varus / valgus stress test in 30° of flexion
Varus/valgus stress test in 90° of flexion

questions.answerText: Varus / valgus stress test in 30° of flexion
questions.explanation:
Main test for MCL (medial collateral ligament) is valgus (abduction) stress in 30° of knee flexion. (Because in full extension it is indicative of combined MCL, posterior oblique ligament injury and posterior cruciate ligament injury).
Varus (Adduction) stress test in 30° flexion (removes the lateral stabilizing effect of iliotibial band so that the lateral collateral ligament can exclusively be examined).

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 13: Sports Injury
questions.stem: A twisting injury of knee in flexed position would result in injury to all except: (AIIMS May 2002)
questions.explanation:
The most common mechanism of ligament disruption of knee is adduction (valgus) flexion and internal rotation of femur on tibia which usually occur in sports in which the foot is planted solidly on the ground and leg is twisted by rotating body (i.e. foot ball, soccer, basket ball, skiing).
The medial structures medial (tibial) collateral ligament (MCL) and medial capsular ligament are first to fail, followed by ACL tears, if the force is of sufficient magnitude.
The medial meniscus may be trapped between condyles and have a peripheral tear, thus producing unhappy triad of O'Donoghue.

Reference: Page 119, Section: COLLATERAL LIGAMENT INJURY & Page 120, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 13: Sports Injury
questions.stem: All are true about menisci of knee joint except: (NEET Pattern 2013)

options.text: Lateral meniscus covers more articular surface of tibia
Lateral meniscus is more prone to injury

questions.answerText: Lateral meniscus is more prone to injury
questions.explanation:
Medial meniscus: Semilunar in shape (less circular), Larger in diameter but narrower in body, Anterior horn is small while posterior horn is large covers less tibial articular surface than lateral (covers about 65% of tibial articular surface), Entire periphery of the meniscus is attached to the joint capsule, Is attached to the medial collateral ligament, Less mobile (due to firmer attachment with joint capsule and medial collateral ligament), More prone to injury (due to reduced mobility). The medial meniscus is three to four times more prone to injury than the lateral meniscus.
Lateral meniscus: Semicircular in shape (C shaped; more circular), Smaller in diameter but wider in body, Anterior horn and posterior horn are uniform in size (covers about 85% of tibial articular surface), Entire periphery of meniscus is not attached to joint capsule (area where the popliteus tendon crosses the joint through the popliteus hiatus is not attached), Is not attached to the lateral collateral ligament, More mobile (due to gaps in attachment with joint capsule and lateral collateral ligament), Less prone to injury (due to increased mobility).

Reference: Page 120, Section: Medial meniscus & Lateral meniscus

B. Noninsertional tendinosis with or without peritendinitis (more common than insertional tendinitis): Involves water shed area of circulation (2-6 cm above the insertion). Seen in runners and jumpers. It is also the commonest site of TA rupture.

Intrinsic weakness of the tendon as a result of repetitive microtrauma and incomplete healing in watershed areas of vascularity predispose to tendon rupture in some more commonly ruptured tendons, including the supraspinatus, biceps, and Achilles tendons.
Most frequent cause of partial or complete rupture of a muscle or tendon is eccentric overload of the muscle tendon unit. One factor contributing to muscle overload is fatigue in runners and jumpers.

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 15: Peripheral Nerve Injury
questions.stem: Saturday night palsy is which type of nerve injury: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
Neuropraxia: Tinel's Sign Negative. It is temporary physiological disruption of nerve impulse conduction. The loss of function is incomplete. Complete recovery takes place in 3-6 weeks and it comes back like lightening, i.e. completely recovers in one go. No Wallerian degeneration takes place and Tinel's sign is negative. Crutch palsy - Pressure palsy (radial nerve or part of brachial plexus injured). Saturday night palsy - Pressure palsy (radial nerve). Tourniquet palsy - Pressure palsy. Few traumatic nerve injuries are neuropraxia.

Reference: Page 148, Section: SEDDONS CLASSIFICATION & Page 154, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 15: Peripheral Nerve Injury
questions.stem: A politician was shot by a gun in back in political rally at T8 level, after which he developed paraplegia. The fact that the injured nerve is not able to regenerate is due to all the reasons except? (AIIMS Nov 2012)
questions.explanation:
Potential ways to improve neuronal regeneration in the CNS: 1. Act on the secondary cell death process: so block apoptosis and help neurons survive. 2. Neurotrophic factors: BDNF (brain derived neurotrophic factor) is the best studied. It does help injured neurons survive. Also helps axons grow. But, should be viewed with caution since injecting a growth factor into the CNS can cause uncontrolled growth (potentially carcinogenic). 3. Remove growth inhibitors: Astrocyte associated: As part of scarring process, astrocytes lay down chondroitan sulfate proteoglycans. The signal from the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans acts as a stop signal for axon growth. Adding a chondroitinase (cleaves off chondroitin-sulfate) promotes axon regrowth in injured area. Myelin-associated inhibitors (from oligodendrocytes): there are 3 diff ones that are all recognized by axons as stop signals: myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), oligodendrocyte myelin glycoprotein (OMgp), and Nogo. A cell surface receptor binds any one of the 3, activates a protein kinase involved in the breakdown of cytoskeletal elements that are needed for process outgrowth. A TAJ knock-out of the myelin associated inhibitors works to inhibit the inhibitor and promote axon growth. 4. PNS nerve graft: Provides basal lamina (called "bands of bungner"). Works to some extent. But, unclear if it is the nerve graft itself that is working, or the fact that you've caused inflammation and subsequently dumped in a bunch of activated macrophages. 5. Glial Scar inhibits nerve regeneration.

Reference: Page 154, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 15: Peripheral Nerve Injury
questions.stem: Which of the following is true about nerve injury? (AIIMS Nov 2012)

options.text: In all cases of open wound with clinical signs of nerve injury, nerve exploration should always be done.
Nerve conduction velocity is best predictor within 48 hrs of injury.
Positive Tine's sign indicates the accurate location of lesion.
Traction nerve injury should be repaired immediately.

questions.answerText: In all cases of open wound with clinical signs of nerve injury, nerve exploration should always be done.
questions.explanation:
Nerve injuries with wound should always be explored and If nerve is in continuity then it is treated like closed injury. If there is clean cut then it is primarily repaired and if ends are crushed debridement is done and then repaired later.
Nerve conduction velocity usually predicts about nerve injury between days 10-14.
Tine's sign can predict about the rate of nerve recovery its speed of regeneration based upon the level of unmyelinated free nerve endings.
Traction nerve injuries are managed with expectant approach of wait and watch for recovery and then if recovery does not take place then it needs exploration and repair.

questions.stem: All are true regarding brachial plexus injury, except: (A12006)

options.text: Preganglionic lesions have a better prognosis than postganglionic lesions
Erb's palsy causes paralysis of the abductors and external rotators of the shoulder
In Klumpe's palsy, Homer's syndrome may be present on the ipsilateral side
Histamine test is useful to differentiate between the preganglionic and postganglionic lesions

questions.answerText: Preganglionic lesions have a better prognosis than postganglionic lesions
questions.explanation:
Feature: Preganglionic Lesion - Proximal to dorsal root ganglion, i.e. avulsion of nerve root from spinal cord; Surgical repair - Irreparable; Prognosis - Poor; Histamine test - Positive.
Feature: Postganglionic - Distal to dorsal root ganglion, i.e. disruption of nerve root (distal), trunk or peripheral nerve; Surgical repair - Reparable; Prognosis - Better; Histamine test - Negative.

Reference: Page 157, Section: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS & Page 151, Section: Feature

Musculocutaneous nerve supplies coracobrachialis, the biceps brachii and the brachialis, and is continued into the forearm as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. questions.explanation:
Axillary Nerve (C5-C6): Injured in fracture of surgical neck humerus and shoulder dislocation (anterior and inferior).
Motor: Deltoid muscle palsy. Loss of rounded contour of shoulder - giving shoulder a flattened appearance and produce hollow inferior to acromion. Weakness of abduction (15°-90°). Ters minor palsy.
Sensory: Lateral cutaneous nerve of arm. Sensory loss over lower half of deltoid (regimental batch area).

Loss of sensation along lateral side of upper arm

questions.explanation:
Abduction of Shoulder: Upto 15° - Supraspinatus muscle - Suprascapular N (C5 C6); 15° to 90° - Deltoid muscle - Axillary nerve (C5 C6); Overhead abduction (>90°) - Serratus anterior muscle (Nerve supply - Long thoracic nerve or N. of Bells - C5 C6 C7) and Trapezius muscle (Spinal part of accessory nerve).
Axillary nerve supplies deltoid which is responsible for shoulder abduction of 15° to 90° so injury to axillary nerve would not affect overhead abduction.

questions.stem: Compression of a nerve within the carpal tunnel produces inability to: (AI 2010, 97 AIIMS May 05, 02, PGI 98)

options.text: Flex the distal phalanx of the thumb

questions.explanation:
Abductor pollicis brevis (producing abduction of thumb) and opponents pollicis (producing opposition of thumb) are paralysed in low median nerve palsy (in carpal tunnel). So, opposition of thumb is lost. Abduction of thumb can be also carried out by abductor pollicis longus supplied by radial nerve. Flexor pollicis longus will be intact to carry out flexion at thumb phalanx as it is supplied by AIN nerve branch of median nerve above carpal tunnel and adductor pollicis will cause adduction as it is supplied by ulnar nerve.

questions.src: Orthopedics Quick Review, 3/e · Chapter 16: Joint Disorders
questions.stem: In Articular cartilage, most active chondrocytes are seen in: (NEET Pattern 2013)
questions.explanation:
There are four zones (layers) of articular cartilage from the articular surface to subchondral bone.
Superficial zone (zone 1): It is the thinnest zone. It consists of two layer: (i) A sheet of densely packed collagen with little polysaccharide and to cells, covers the joint surface, and (ii) Flattened ellipsoid-shaped chondrocytes, with their major axis parallel to joint surface.
Transition zone (Zone 2): Composition is intermediate between superficial zone and middle zone.
Middle zone or radial zone or deep zone (Zone 3): The chondrocytes are spheroidal in shape with their major axis perpendicular to joint surface. Chondrocytes are most active synthetically in this zone. This zone contains the largest diameter collagen fibrils, the highest concentration of proteoglycans and the lowest concentration of water.
Calcified cartilage zone (Zone 4): It separates the middle zone from subchondral bone. The cells are small with small amount of endoplasmic reticulum and golgi apparatus with very little metabolic activity. Cells are surrounded by calcified cartilage.
